title: ISC U1·W1 — IT Governance, COBIT & the IT Environment (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — who controls the systems

The Information Systems and Controls (ISC) discipline tests how an organization governs, secures, and controls the technology that produces its financial and operational data. Meridian Building Group runs its job-cost, payroll, and billing on integrated systems; if those systems are poorly governed, every number they produce is suspect. This week establishes the IT governance frameworks, the structure of the IT function, and the control environment that the rest of the discipline builds on — the systems analogue to the conceptual framework that opens FAR.

IT governance versus IT management

IT governance is the board-and-executive responsibility to ensure technology aligns with business strategy, delivers value, and manages risk — distinct from IT management, which runs day-to-day operations. Governance asks "are we doing the right things, and are risks acceptable?"; management asks "are we doing them well?" Effective governance sets the direction (strategy, risk appetite, investment priorities) and monitors outcomes, while delegating execution. The separation mirrors COSO's governance-and-culture component and is the foundation for everything from access control to SOC reporting.

The COBIT framework

COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies) is the leading framework for governing and managing enterprise IT. It distinguishes governance objectives (evaluate, direct, monitor) from management objectives (plan, build, run, monitor), and organizes IT activities into domains with measurable control objectives. COBIT's principles stress that the governance system should be tailored to the enterprise, cover it end-to-end, and be driven by stakeholder needs. It is the framework most directly tied to the ISC discipline's governance content, complementing COSO (enterprise risk/internal control) and operational frameworks like ITIL.

The control environment for IT

IT controls rest on a sound control environment: the tone set by governance, an organizational structure with clear authority and responsibility, competent personnel, and accountability. A central principle is segregation of incompatible IT duties — separating systems development from computer operations, and both from security administration, so that no one can write code, move it to production, and run it without independent checks. Where the organization is too small to fully separate duties, compensating controls (management review of logs and exception reports) substitute. This environment makes the specific general and application controls trustworthy.

Organizing the IT function

A typical IT function separates roles to enforce segregation. Systems analysts and application programmers design and build software; computer operators run production jobs; database administrators (DBAs) control the data structures and access; network and security administrators manage connectivity and protections; and a help desk supports users. The key incompatibility to avoid is letting programmers have access to production data and programs — a programmer who can both write and deploy code can introduce unauthorized changes. Governance assigns these roles and reviews that the separations hold.

IT risk and the frameworks that address it

IT risk spans availability, integrity, confidentiality, and compliance — a system outage, corrupted data, a breach, or a regulatory failure each threatens the business. Several frameworks address it: COBIT (governance/management of IT), COSO (enterprise risk management and internal control), ITIL (IT service management), the NIST cybersecurity framework, and ISO/IEC 27001 (information-security management). A mature organization maps its controls to one or more frameworks so that risks are identified, owned, and monitored rather than addressed ad hoc.

Governance bodies and IT strategy

Governance is exercised through structures: the board (or audit committee) oversees IT risk, often informed by an IT steering committee that prioritizes investments and aligns projects with strategy. An IT strategic plan translates business goals into a technology roadmap, and policies (acceptable use, security, change management) set the rules of the road. These structures ensure that major decisions — adopting a new ERP, moving to the cloud, investing in analytics — are made deliberately, with risk and value weighed, rather than left to technical staff alone.

Governing emerging technology

New technologies stretch governance. Cloud computing shifts infrastructure to third parties, making vendor and SOC-report oversight (covered later in this discipline) essential. Artificial intelligence and automation raise questions of model risk, bias, and explainability. Robotic process automation (RPA) and APIs change how data flows between systems. The governance response is the same in principle: define ownership, assess risk, set controls and monitoring, and keep the technology aligned with strategy and risk appetite — the discipline's recurring theme that control follows from governance.

Comparing the major frameworks

Because the frameworks overlap, knowing each one's focus prevents confusion. COBIT governs and manages enterprise IT end-to-end. COSO's frameworks address internal control and enterprise risk management broadly, with IT as one element. ITIL is operational — it structures IT service management (incident, problem, and change processes). The NIST Cybersecurity Framework organizes security around identify, protect, detect, respond, recover. ISO/IEC 27001 certifies an information-security management system. A useful mental model: COBIT and COSO sit at the governance level, ITIL at the service level, and NIST/ISO at the security level — and a mature organization draws on several at once rather than treating them as competitors.

Outsourcing and third-party governance

Governance does not stop at the organization's walls. When MBG outsources hosting, payroll, or an application to a service organization, it remains accountable for the controls over its data even though it does not operate them. Governance therefore extends to vendor management: due diligence before engagement, contractual control requirements and service-level agreements, and ongoing monitoring — including obtaining and reading the provider's SOC reports (the focus of the next ISC unit). The principle is that responsibility cannot be outsourced: the organization must govern the risk wherever its data lives, including in the cloud and across its supply chain.

Monitoring and continuous improvement

Governance is not a one-time design — it requires monitoring. The board and steering committee track IT performance against objectives using metrics (system availability, project delivery, incident counts, audit findings), review the results of internal and external assessments, and direct remediation of deficiencies. Frameworks like COBIT build in a monitor domain precisely so that the governance system evaluates and improves itself over time. This continuous loop — direct, do, monitor, correct — is what keeps IT aligned with the business as both the technology and the strategy change.

CMA bridge

The CMA program treated MBG's systems as the source of its management data; ISC governs whether those systems can be trusted. The segregation of development from operations is exactly what lets a CFO rely on a system-generated WIP or payroll number — governance is what turns raw system output into reliable information.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish IT governance (board/executive: align, value, risk — evaluate/direct/monitor) from IT management (run operations).
  2. Apply COBIT (governance vs management objectives; tailored, end-to-end, stakeholder-driven) alongside COSO, ITIL, NIST, and ISO 27001.
  3. Enforce the control environment: segregate systems development, operations, and security; keep programmers out of production; use compensating controls when small.
  4. Govern through structures (board/audit committee, IT steering committee, strategic plan, policies) — including for cloud, AI, and RPA.

Recap: IT governance is the board-and-executive duty to align technology with strategy, deliver value, and manage risk (evaluate/direct/monitor), distinct from day-to-day IT management; COBIT is the leading IT-governance framework, complemented by COSO, ITIL, NIST, and ISO 27001; a sound control environment segregates systems development, operations, and security (keeping programmers out of production) with compensating controls when duties cannot be split; and governance is exercised through the board, an IT steering committee, a strategic plan, and policies that extend to emerging technology like cloud, AI, and RPA.

questions.q: IT governance is primarily concerned with:
choices: Aligning IT with strategy and managing risk (evaluate/direct/monitor)
questions.explain: Governance is the board/executive responsibility to align IT with strategy, deliver value, and manage risk; management runs operations.

questions.q: COBIT is best described as a framework for:
questions.explain: COBIT governs and manages enterprise IT, separating governance from management objectives.

questions.q: The most critical IT segregation of duties keeps:
choices: Programmers out of production data and programs
questions.explain: A programmer with production access could deploy unauthorized code, so development and operations must be separated.

questions.q: Which framework focuses specifically on information-security management?
questions.explain: ISO/IEC 27001 is the information-security management standard; ITIL is service management; COBIT governs IT broadly.

questions.q: When a small company cannot fully segregate IT duties, it should rely on:
choices: Compensating controls such as management review of logs
questions.explain: Compensating controls (review of logs/exception reports) substitute when duties cannot be separated.

choices: Prioritizes IT investments and aligns projects with strategy
questions.explain: The steering committee is a governance body aligning IT investment with business strategy.

questions.q: The database administrator's role is incompatible with:
questions.explain: Combining DBA access with programming would let one person both design data structures and alter the programs that use them.
